newsitem.title: USA: U.S. exporters say China soy purchase makes sense.
newsitem.headline: U.S. exporters say China soy purchase makes sense.

text.p: U.S. exporters said Chinese buyers have been in the U.S. soybean market recently and a sale of new-crop soybeans would make sense although they could not confirm such a deal.
Exporters said a new-crop sale would not be surprising because Chinese buyers had been inquiring for October and November positions.
Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures sped higher early amid talk China bought about 50,000 tonnes each of old- and new-crop soybeans and a similar amount of old-crop soymeal.
At 1000 CDT, CBOT August soybeans were up 19 cents at $7.16 per bushel and November soybeans were up 11-3/4 at $5.96. CBOT August soymeal was up $5.40 at $231.80 per ton.
U.S. exporters said China buying of new-crop U.S. soybeans would make sense, but doubted China would buy the more expensive old-crop U.S. soybeans.
"I find it hard to believe. It doesn't make sense to me," said one exporter of an old-crop sale to China.
U.S. soybeans for August shipment were priced about $30 per ton higher in U.S. Gulf CIF market than for last-half September soybeans, U.S. dealers said.
"They were looking and prices were down," said another exporter. However, he also could not confirm a sale.

Although traders questioned the feasibility of an old-crop sale due to prices, some grain market analysts said the recent sharp drop in U.S. old-crop soybean prices would make a sale to China believable.
"We are competitive," said Fred Sonenson, analyst with LFG LLC.
Soneson said the price premium of old-crop soybeans to new-crop would not be a deterrent to a sale.
"Every so often you have to pay for something, not because of the price but because you need it," he said.

CBOT traders also said U.S. soybeans for August delivery were priced competitively with South American supplies. Archer Daniels Midland Inc, Cargill Inc, Produce Grain and Term Commodities were all small-lot buyers of the August soybeans, traders said.
While trade talk circulated that China had also bought a cargo of soymeal, Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney, doubted such a deal because Brazil soymeal was about $35 per ton less expensive.
"The meal makes absolutely no sense," he said.
On Monday, there were hints in the CBOT soybean market that a soybean deal was in the works. Commercial firms were small-scale buyers of the August which contributed to the gains.
